nodes.title: The two arms are strongly correlated per round: a2 passes 73.5% when a1 passes and 18.8% when a1 fails
nodes.body: Replayed 225 two-arm rounds (research/exp/e30.mjs): a1 passed 115 times. Given a1 passed, a2 also passed 73.5% of the time; given a1 failed, a2 passed only 18.8% (21 rescues out of 110). The arms are the same model with the same prompt, so the correlation is round-level difficulty showing through both samples - which means the second arm is not an independent bet, and 'rescue the failed round' is the expensive case, not the common one. Policy comparison on recorded outcomes: fixed K=1 gives 113 successes for 225 arms (1.99 arms per success); fixed K=2 gives 134 for 450 (3.36); sequential 'run the second only if the first failed' gives 134 for 337 (2.52). So sequential-if-failed captures the entire benefit of the second arm for 25% fewer attempts than fixed K=2, but the second arm still costs 26% more arms per success than not having it. This is the first measured policy comparison for this loop, and it needs no model calls to compute.

nodes.title: Because arms correlate within a round, any A/B that holds the round fixed is measuring round difficulty, not the treatment
nodes.body: exp-slot-004 gives the mechanism behind three earlier results that looked like noise. Paired within-round comparisons (exp-lesson-001, lesson.impact) hold the round fixed, so both arms share the round's difficulty; when the round is easy both pass and the delta is 0 (53 of 60 cases), when it is hard both fail (also 0), and a nonzero delta appears only in the narrow band where the arms disagree - which is exactly where the tie-break then decides who wins (exp-slot-001). So a within-round paired design is not a low-power design here, it is a confounded one: it is conditioned on a variable that drives both outcomes. A usable design has to randomise the treatment across rounds (switchback, exp-human-002) or compare across campaigns, and must report the round-difficulty strata rather than a pooled mean.
